04

Theory of Bending

A loaded beam carries two kinds of stress. The bending stress σ comes from the bending moment, and the shear stress τ comes from the shear force. This section builds the bending equation, σ = M·y / I, from first principles. The shear stress formula, τ = V·Q / (I·b), follows after the bending problems.

A beam and its plane of symmetry

Fig 1 shows a beam with a vertical plane of symmetry. The loads act in this plane. Under end moments M the beam bends into a circular arc, and the cross-sections at the two ends tilt but stay plane (Fig 2).

Concept of pure bending

A beam segment is in pure bending when the internal bending moment is constant along its length and the shear force is zero. No transverse load acts within that segment, only end couples. This is the idealised condition the classical bending equation is derived for. Two examples:

Example 1: a couple M at the free end of a cantilever gives zero shear force everywhere and a constant bending moment M along the whole length. Example 2: two equal loads P a distance l from the supports of a simply supported beam. Between the loads the shear force is zero and the bending moment is constant.

Assumptions of the theory of bending

The derivation rests on six assumptions, all of which must hold for the equation below to be valid:

This keeps the section properties (I, y) constant along x, so a single bending equation applies everywhere.

Simplifies the problem to two dimensions, so bending occurs only in the plane containing all the loads.

Keeps the loading symmetric about the beam, so it bends in that plane without twisting or bending sideways.

Distinguishes pure bending problems from beams that are actually governed by shear failure or buckling.

Uniform E means stress is directly proportional to strain everywhere in the section, in both tension and compression zones.

This is the core kinematic assumption behind the whole derivation. It is what makes strain vary linearly with distance from the neutral axis.

Derivation of the bending equation

The derivation has three parts: find the strain in a fibre, find the moment the stresses in the section provide, then combine the two.

1

Strain in a fibre at distance y from the neutral surface

Fibre AB lies at distance y below the neutral surface (Fig 1a). When the beam bends into an arc of radius R (Fig 1b), fibre AB stretches to A′B′ while the neutral fibre CD keeps its length.

  1. Strain in fibre AB = change in length / original length = (A′B′ − AB) / AB, and AB = CD = C′D′.
  2. So strain = (A′B′ − C′D′) / C′D′ = [(R + y)θ − Rθ] / Rθ = y / R.
  3. Since stress / strain = E, σ/E = y/R, so σ / y = E / R  …(1)
2

Moment of resistance of the cross-section

Take a thin strip of area δA at distance y from the neutral axis (N.A.). Add up the moments of the forces on all such strips.

  1. Force on the strip: F = σ·δA = (E/R)·y·δA.
  2. Moment of this force about the N.A. = F·y = (E/R)·y²·δA.
  3. Total moment over the whole cross-section: M = Σ(E/R)·y²δA = (E/R)·Σy²δA = (E/R)·I.
  4. So M / I = E / R  …(2)
3

Combine equations (1) and (2)

Equations (1) and (2) share the ratio E/R, so they combine into one statement:

The Bending Equation
σ / y = M / I = E / R
σ bending stress at distance y from the neutral axis  ·  y distance from the neutral axis  ·  M bending moment at the section  ·  I second moment of area (moment of inertia) about the neutral axis  ·  E Young’s modulus  ·  R radius of curvature

Neutral axis (N.A.)

The axis at which the bending stress is zero is the neutral axis. It always passes through the centroid of the cross-section, and it separates the tension zone from the compression zone.

At the neutral axis
σ = 0

Section modulus, Z

The section modulus is the ratio of the moment of inertia of a section about its neutral axis to the distance of the outermost layer from the neutral axis. It is denoted by Z. It packages the geometry of a cross-section into a single number for quick strength comparisons.

From the bending equation to Z
σ / y = M / I
σ = (M / I)·y
σmax = (Mmax / I)·ymax
σmax = Mmax / Z
Definition
Z = I / ymax
Section Modulus — Common Sections
Rectangle: Z = b·d²/6    Solid circle: Z = π·d³/32
For a rectangle, Z = I / ymax = (b·d³/12) / (d/2) = b·d²/6. A higher Z for the same cross-sectional area means a stronger, more material-efficient section. This is why I-sections outperform solid rectangles in bending.

06

Shear Stress in Beams

Bending isn't the only stress in a loaded beam. Wherever shear force exists, shear stress develops across the cross-section too. For a section of width b at distance y from the neutral axis, with shaded area A above that level and centroid distance ȳ from the neutral axis:

General Shear Stress Formula
τ = F · Aȳ / (I · b)
F shear force   A area above the level considered   ȳ centroid distance of that area from the N.A.   I moment of inertia of the whole section   b width at the level considered

The distribution this formula produces is never uniform. It depends on how the width b and the shaded area change with y, which is why the shape of the cross-section changes the whole picture.

Derivation of the shear stress formula

1

Set-up: two sections a small distance dx apart

Take sections AB and CD a distance dx apart. At AB the shear force is F and the bending moment is M. At CD they are F + dF and M + dM. Consider an elemental cylinder of area dA and length dx, at distance y from the neutral axis.

  1. Let σ = intensity of bending stress on the end of the cylinder at AB, and σ + dσ = intensity at CD.
  2. From the bending equation, M/I = σ/y, so σ = (M / I)·y.
2

Net unbalanced force on the elemental cylinder

  1. Stress at AB: σ = (M/I)·y. Stress at CD: σ + dσ = ((M + dM)/I)·y.
  2. Force on the end at AB = σ·dA = (M/I)·y·dA. Force on the end at CD = ((M + dM)/I)·y·dA.
  3. Net unbalanced force on the cylinder = ((M + dM)/I)·y·dA − (M/I)·y·dA = (dM / I)·y·dA.
3

Add up over the area above the level EF, then equate to the shear force

  1. Total unbalanced force on all elements above EF = ∫(dM/I)·y·dA = (dM/I)·∫y·dA = (dM / I)·A·ȳ.
  2. Here A is the area of the section above the level EF, and ȳ is the distance of its centroid from the neutral axis.
  3. Let τ = intensity of horizontal shear at EF and b = width of the beam at EF. The shear area is b·dx, so the shear force is τ·b·dx.
  4. Equating: τ·b·dx = (dM/I)·A·ȳ, so τ = (dM/dx)·(A·ȳ / (I·b)). Since dM/dx = F, τ = F·A·ȳ / (I·b).

Shear stress distribution by cross-section

For a rectangle of width b and depth d, the shear stress distribution across the depth is parabolic. It is zero at the top and bottom fibres and maximum at the neutral axis.

Result
τmax = 1.5 × τavg
Working
  1. The shaded area above level EF, at distance y from the N.A., is A = b·(d/2 − y). Its centroid is at ȳ = y + ½(d/2 − y) = ½(d/2 + y).
  2. Substituting into τ = F·A·ȳ / (I·b) gives τ = (F / 2I)·(d²/4 − y²), a parabola in y.
  3. At the top edge, y = d/2, so τ = 0.
  4. At the neutral axis, y = 0, so τ = F·d² / 8I. With I = b·d³/12 this is 1.5·F / (b·d).
  5. The average shear stress is τavg = shear force / area of section = F / (b·d). Therefore τmax = 1.5 × τavg.

For a solid circular section of radius R, the same integration gives a parabolic distribution as well, but with a different peak-to-average ratio because the width varies with y along a curved boundary.

Result
τmax = (4/3) × τavg
Working
  1. Take a strip of thickness dy at distance y from the N.A. Its width is EF = 2·EB = 2√(R² − y²), so dA = 2√(R² − y²)·dy.
  2. The moment of this strip about the N.A. is y·dA = 2y√(R² − y²)·dy.
  3. Integrating for the whole shaded area, from y to R: A·ȳ = ∫yR 2y√(R² − y²)·dy = (2/3)·(R² − y²)3/2.
  4. With b = 2√(R² − y²): τ = F·A·ȳ / (I·b) = (F / 3I)·(R² − y²), a parabola in y.
  5. At the neutral axis (y = 0): τmax = F·R² / 3I. With I = πD&sup4;/64 = πR&sup4;/4 this gives τmax = (4/3)·F / (πR²).
  6. The average shear stress is τavg = F / (πR²), so τmax = (4/3) × τavg.
Lecture derivation, in order

An I-section behaves very differently: the wide flanges carry almost no shear (the width B is large, so τ stays small), while the narrow web carries the overwhelming majority of the shear force. This is exactly why I-beams are so efficient. The flanges resist bending, and the web resists shear.

Result
τweb,max ≫ τflange
Working

Let B = overall width of the section, D = overall depth, b = thickness of the web, and d = depth of the web. The shear stress at distance y from the N.A. is τ = F·A·ȳ / (I·b).

(i) In the flange (width B)

  1. Shaded area A = B·(D/2 − y). Its centroid is ȳ = y + ½(D/2 − y) = ½(D/2 + y).
  2. τ = F·A·ȳ / (I·B) = (F / 2I)·(D²/4 − y²). The variation with y is parabolic, and τ decreases as y increases.
  3. Upper edge of the flange, y = D/2: τ = 0.
  4. Lower edge of the flange, y = d/2: τ = (F / 8I)·(D² − d²).

(ii) In the web (width b)

  1. A·ȳ is the moment of the flange area about the N.A. plus the moment of the shaded web area: A·ȳ = (B/8)·(D² − d²) + (b/2)·(d²/4 − y²).
  2. τ = F / (I·b) × [(B/8)(D² − d²) + (b/2)(d²/4 − y²)]. Again parabolic in y.
  3. At the neutral axis, y = 0: τmax = F / (I·b) × [B(D² − d²)/8 + b·d²/8].
  4. At the top of the web (junction with the flange), y = d/2: τ = F·B·(D² − d²) / (8·I·b).

At the junction the stress on the flange side is (F/8I)(D² − d²), and on the web side it is B/b times larger, because the width drops from B to b. This is the sudden jump in the distribution figure.

Lecture derivation, in order

Problem 25 — Rectangular section: shear stress 25 mm above the N.A.

A wooden beam 100 mm wide and 150 mm deep is simply supported over a span of 4 metres. If shear force at a section of the beam is 4500 N, find the shear stress at a distance of 25 mm above the N.A.

Given
Width, b
100 mm
Depth, d
150 mm
Span
4 m, simply supported
Shear force, F
4500 N
To find

The shear stress at 25 mm above the neutral axis.

Answer. τ = 4500 × 5000 × 50 / (28125000 × 100) = 0.4 N/mm2 at 25 mm above the N.A.

Worked solution (from the lecture)

Problem 26 — Rectangular beam: average, maximum and intermediate shear stress

A rectangular beam 100 mm wide and 250 mm deep is subjected to a maximum shear force of 50 kN. Determine: (i) average shear stress, (ii) maximum shear stress, (iii) shear stress at a distance of 25 mm above the neutral axis.

Given
Width, b
100 mm
Depth, d
250 mm
Maximum shear force, F
50 kN = 50,000 N
To find

(i) τavg, (ii) τmax, (iii) τ at y = 25 mm above the N.A.

Answer. (i) τavg = F / (b·d) = 2 N/mm2. (ii) τmax = 1.5 × τavg = 3 N/mm2. (iii) τ = (F/2I)(d²/4 − y²) = 2.88 N/mm2 at y = 25 mm.

Worked solution (from the lecture)

Problem 27 — Timber beam: ratio of span to depth

A timber beam of rectangular section is simply supported at the ends and carries a point load at the centre of the beam. The maximum bending stress is 12 N/mm2 and maximum shearing stress is 1 N/mm2, find the ratio of the span to the depth.

Given
Maximum bending stress
12 N/mm2
Maximum shear stress
1 N/mm2
Loading
Point load W at the centre, span L
Reactions
RA = RB = W/2
To find

The ratio L / d of span to depth.

Answer. From the shear condition, τmax = 1.5 × W/(2bd) = 1, so W/(bd) = 4/3. From the bending condition, σmax = 1.5·W·L / (b·d²) = 12. Combining these gives L / d = 6.

Worked solution (from the lecture)

Problem 28 — Wooden beam: safe load W

A simply supported wooden beam of span 1.3 m having a cross-section 150 mm wide by 250 mm deep carries a point load W at the centre. The permissible stresses are 7 N/mm2 in bending and 1 N/mm2 in shearing. Calculate the safe load W.

Given
Span
1.3 m, simply supported
Section
150 mm wide × 250 mm deep
Permissible stresses
7 N/mm2 in bending, 1 N/mm2 in shearing
Loading
Point load W at the centre
To find

The safe load W. It must satisfy both the bending limit and the shear limit, so the smaller of the two values governs.

08

Beam of Uniform Strength

A beam of uniform strength has the same maximum bending stress along the whole length of the beam.

In an ordinary prismatic cantilever, the bending moment (and so the bending stress) is highest at the fixed support and falls to zero at the free end, yet the cross-section stays the same size along the whole length. Most of that material near the free end is doing very little work.

A beam of uniform strength is shaped so that σmax = M/Z is the same at every cross-section. Since M falls off toward the free end, the section modulus Z is allowed to fall off in step with it, by tapering the depth, the width, or both along the length.

Design Condition
σmax = Mmax / Z
M(x) / Z(x) = σallow = constant
Solving this for Z(x), and hence for b(x) or d(x), gives the taper profile. For a cantilever with a tip load W, a rectangular section of constant width tapers in depth as d(x) ∝ √x from the free end.
Section Modulus of a Rectangular Section
Z = I / ymax = (b·d³/12) / (d/2) = b·d² / 6
The same definition of section modulus, Z = I / ymax, used in the theory of bending above.

This is the same principle behind the tapered look of leaf springs, aircraft wing spars, and diving boards. Each section uses only as much material as it actually needs.
